translation_en:
Cheng Wanzhong 程萬鍾 (registered in a salt-producer household in Fushun County, Xuzhou Prefecture, Sichuan; National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Changes [Yijing]; courtesy name Tingxi; seniority first; age thirty-five, born on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month). His great-grandfather was Cheng Xingzu, his grandfather was Cheng Wenlong, his father was Cheng Wei, and his mother is née Xia. His mother is living. He married née Ye. He placed 17th in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 270th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Kan Nai 闞鼐 (registered in an official household in Luanzhou, Yongping Prefecture, Zhili; National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Zhongfu; seniority seventh; age twenty-nine, born on the eighth day of the fourth month). His great-grandfather was Kan Liulang; his grandfather was Kan Congde (posthumously honoured as General of Martial Virtue); his father was Kan Tai (Battalion Commander of the Right Battalion of the Yongqing Guard); and his mother is née Li (invested as Lady of Suitability). His mother is living. His elder brothers are Kan Ming, Kan Zhen, Kan Duo, Kan Zhong, Kan Jian, and Kan Ding; his younger brother is Kan Zi (Company Commander). He married née Yang. He placed 29th in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 256th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Yan 陳儼 (registered in a wealthy household in Wanping County, Shuntian Prefecture, originally from Luling County, Jiangxi; National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Shizhuang; seniority fourth; age twenty-nine, born on the twenty-sixth day of the sixth month). His great-grandfather was Chen Zilong; his grandfather was Chen Sixing; his father is Chen Tinghuan; his father's first wife was née Liu, his birth mother was née Gao, and his stepmother is née Liu. His father and stepmother are both living. His younger brother is Chen Xi. He married née Xiao, and remarried née Song. He placed 21st in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 289th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Yu 劉瑜 (registered in a civilian household in Anfu County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi; County School Student; specialized in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Yanzhuo; seniority first; age thirty-three, born on the fifteenth day of the eighth month). His great-grandfather was Liu Yuanyuan, his grandfather is Liu Zhongwen, his father is Liu Shigang, and his mother is née Peng. Both his parents and grandparents are living. His younger brothers are Liu Chen and Liu Can. He married née He. He placed 129th in the [illegible; Jiangxi Provincial Examination?] and 203rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Li Zhigang 李志綱, registered under a saltern household in Neijiang County, Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan, was a National University Student (guozisheng) specializing in the Classic of History (Shujing). His style name was Zhenji, he was the third in his generation, and he was twenty-four years old, born on the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Li Wensheng (a Yuan-dynasty Intendant [tiju]); his grandfather was Li Guoyan; his father is Li Yanshi; and his mother is née Zhang. Both of his parents are living; he has elder brothers Zhichang and Zhilian, and a younger brother Zhihui; he is married to née Liu. He placed 16th in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 231st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xiong Hui 熊惠, registered under a military household of the Embroidered-uniform Guard (Jinyiwei) and originally from Nanchang County, Jiangxi, was a Military Student of the Shuntian Prefectural School specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing). His style name was Diji, he was the second in his generation, and he was thirty years old, born on the ninth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Xiong Zongwen; his grandfather was Xiong Xixuan; his father is Xiong Haoran; and his mother is née Chen. Both of his parents are living; he has an elder brother Zhongfu, and younger brothers Zhongyou and Zhongzuo; he married née Chen and remarried née Zhang. He placed 127th in the Shuntian Provincial Examination and 100th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Han Yin 韓殷, registered under a civilian household in Panyu County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, was a National University Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His style name was Fumin, he was the first in his generation, and he was thirty years old, born on the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Han Zisui; his grandfather was Han Suichu; his father is Han Chang; his father's former wife was née Liu; and his mother is née Pan. Both of his parents are living; he has younger brothers Yan, Wei, and Tong; he is married to née Jian. He placed 60th in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 102nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou晟 周晟 (Zhou Sheng), registered under a military household in She County, Cizhou Department, Zhangde Prefecture, Henan, was a National University Student specializing in the Classic of History. His style name was Deming, he was the first in his generation, and he was twenty-six years old, born on the fifth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Zhou Tingyuan; his grandfather is Zhou Cheng (invested as Investigating Censor [jiancha yushi]); his father is Zhou Hao (Investigating Censor); and his mother is née Song (invested as Child Nurturer [ruren]). Both his parents and grandparents are living; he has younger brothers Sheng, Chang, Mian, Yu, and Jing; he married née Shen and remarried née Liu. He placed 34th in the Henan Provincial Examination and 286th in the Metropolitan Examination.

貫順天府懷柔縣軍籍　縣學生

周一清〔貫浙江台州府臨海縣，府學增廣生，治《詩經》，字廉夫，行一，年三十三，四月十二日生〕。曾祖叔佐；祖宗溥〔知縣〕；父克靜，母金氏，繼母杜氏、羅氏、倪氏。具慶下，弟一夔、一本、一誠，娶陳氏。浙江鄉試第五十三名，會試第一百八十二名。

王度〔貫江西吉安府吉水縣民籍，縣學生，治《詩經》，字洪量，行三，年四十八，十一月二十日生〕。曾祖所安；祖子通；父嘉謀，母周氏。永感下，兄洪舒、洪惟，弟洪宣、洪裕、洪鈞、洪緒，娶廖氏。江西鄉試第八名，會試第二百三十八名。

王詔〔貫順天府懷柔縣軍籍，縣學生，治《詩經》，字廷徵，行一，年二十九，十月十七日生〕。曾祖德彬；祖甫義；父禮〔府知事〕，叔恂〔前吏部主事〕，母牛氏。嚴侍下，娶李氏，繼娶沈氏、萬氏。順天府鄉試第五十名，會試第六十四名。

王上齡〔貫山西大同府渾源州軍籍，州學增廣生，治《春秋》，字大壽，行三，年二十三，五月二十九日生〕。曾祖廣；祖才甫；父懋〔知縣〕，母裴氏。具慶下，兄延齡、昌齡，未娶。山西鄉試第二名，會試第二百十二名。
translation_en:
Zhou Yiqing 周一清, courtesy name Lianfu 廉夫, first in seniority among his brothers, aged thirty-three, born on the twelfth day of the fourth month, was registered in Linhai County, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. He was anAdded Student at the Prefectural School specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing). His great-grandfather was Zhou Shuzuo; his grandfather was Zhou Zongpu, who served as a County Magistrate; his father was Zhou Kejing; his mother was née Jin; and his stepmothers were née Du, née Luo, and née Ni. Both his father and stepmother were living. His younger brothers were Yikui, Yiben, and Yicheng, and he was married to née Chen. He placed fifty-third in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and one hundred eighty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Du 王度, courtesy name Hongliang 洪量, third in seniority among his brothers, aged forty-eight, born on the twentieth day of the eleventh month, was registered in a civilian household in Jishui County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi. He was a County School Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing). His great-grandfather was Wang Suo'an; his grandfather was Wang Zitong; his father was Wang Jiamou; and his mother was née Zhou. Both his parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Hongshu and Hongwei, his younger brothers were Hongxuan, Hongyu, Hongjun, and Hongxu, and he was married to née Liao. He placed eighth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and two hundred thirty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Zhao 王詔, courtesy name Tingzheng 廷徵, first in seniority among his brothers, aged twenty-nine, born on the seventeenth day of the tenth month, was registered in a military household in Huairou County, Shuntian Prefecture. He was a County School Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing). His great-grandfather was Wang Debin; his grandfather was Wang Fuyi; his father was Wang Li, a Prefectural Administrative Clerk; his younger paternal uncle was Wang Xun, a former Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel; and his mother was née Niu. His father was living and his mother deceased. He was married to née Li, and subsequently married née Shen and née Wan. He placed fiftieth in the Shuntian Prefectural Examination and sixty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Shangling 王上齡, courtesy name Dashou 大壽, third in seniority among his brothers, aged twenty-three, born on the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month, was registered in a military household in Hunyuan Subprefecture, Datong Prefecture, Shanxi. He was an Added Student at the Subprefectural School specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). His great-grandfather was Wang Guang; his grandfather was Wang Caifu; his father was Wang Mao, a County Magistrate; and his mother was née Pei. Both his parents were living. His elder brothers were Yanling and Changling, and he was unmarried. He placed second in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and two hundred twelfth in the Metropolitan Examination.

沈譓〔貫直隸廬州府合肥縣軍籍，國子生，治《易經》，字用正，行三，年二十七，正月初七日生〕。曾祖顏先，祖博，父容，母馬氏。具慶下。兄誼、讓，弟譚。娶張氏。應天府鄉試第八十四名，會試第二百五十八名。
translation_en:
Niu Xuan 牛宣, courtesy name Dehong 德弘, first in seniority among his brothers, aged twenty-five, born on the fifth day of the third month, was registered as a hereditary military officer in the Chengdu Left Escort Guard (Chengdu zuo huwei 成都左護衛) in Sichuan, and served as a military student at the Huayang County School (Huayang xianxue 華陽縣學), specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing). His great-grandfather was Niu Haigui 海貴, his grandfather Niu Weixin 維新, his paternal uncle Niu Zhong 衷 (a Guard Platoon Commander [wei baihu 衛百戶]), his father Niu Xiang 襄, and his mother Lady Zhao 趙氏. Both his parents and grandparents were living; he was married to Lady Geng 耿氏. He placed 68th in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 143rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yu Ji 俞紀, courtesy name Xianzhou 憲周, second in seniority among his brothers, aged thirty-two, born on the thirtieth day of the second month, was registered in a civilian household of Suining County 遂寧縣 in Tongchuan Subprefecture 潼川州, Sichuan, and served as an added student (zengguangsheng 增廣生) at the county school, specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing). His great-grandfather was Yu Shicong 仕聰, his grandfather Yu Congzheng 從政, his father Yu Xin 信, and his mother Lady Xu 徐氏. His mother was living and his father deceased; his elder brother was Zhisgang 志剛, his younger brothers were Guanzhe 貫哲, Guanshu 貫書, and Guanru 貫儒, and he was married to Lady Tan 譚氏. He placed 8th in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 336th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Fu 沈黻, courtesy name Shubian 叔辯, second in seniority among his brothers, aged thirty-six, born on the twenty-ninth day of the third month, was registered in a civilian household of Huating County 華亭縣 in Songjiang Prefecture 松江府, Southern Metropolitan Area (Zhili 直隸), and served as an added student at the prefectural school, specializing in the Classic of Documents (Shujing). His great-grandfather was Shen Zhongliang 仲良, his grandfather Shen Su 肅, his father Shen Yong 鏞, and his mother Lady Gao 高氏. Both his parents were living; his elder brothers were Ling 齡 and Lun 綸, and he was married to Lady Yu 俞氏. He placed 56th in the Yingtian Prefecture 應天府 Provincial Examination and 228th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Hui 沈譓, courtesy name Yongzheng 用正, third in seniority among his brothers, aged twenty-seven, born on the seventh day of the first month, was registered in a military household of Hefei County 合肥縣 in Luzhou Prefecture 廬州府, Southern Metropolitan Area (Zhili 直隸), and was a student of the Directorate of Education (Guozisheng 國子生), specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing). His great-grandfather was Shen Yanxian 顏先, his grandfather Shen Bo 博, his father Shen Rong 容, and his mother Lady Ma 馬氏. Both his parents were living; his elder brothers were Yi 誼 and Rang 讓, his younger brother was Tan 譚, and he was married to Lady Zhang 張氏. He placed 84th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 258th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰朕以眇躬祗膺
天命纘承
祖宗大業臨御兆民顧惟負
荷之艱莫究弛張之善肆
虛心於宵旰冀資弼於忠
===
良固聖賢樂受盡言在堯
舜惟急先務何則天下之
本莫有外於家國兵民朕
欲聞其至計何先切望何
最君心之發莫有著於禮

良固聖賢樂受盡言在堯
舜惟急先務何則天下之
本莫有外於家國兵民朕
欲聞其至計何先切望何
最君心之發莫有著於禮
punctuated: 皇帝制曰：「朕以眇躬，祗膺天命，纘承祖宗大業，臨御兆民。顧惟負荷之艱，莫究弛張之善，肆虛心於宵旰，冀資弼於忠良。固聖賢樂受盡言，在堯、舜惟急先務。何則？天下之本，莫有外於家國、兵民，朕欲聞其至計何先、切望何最？君心之發，莫有著於禮
translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: "With Our humble person, We have reverently received the Mandate of Heaven, succeeded to the great enterprise of Our Imperial Ancestors, and come to rule over the millions of the common people. Reflecting upon the difficulty of bearing this burden, and unable to fathom the best way of balancing leniency and rigor in governance, We keep an open mind while laboring from before dawn until after dark, hoping to rely on the assistance of the loyal and worthy. Truly, sages and worthies delight in receiving unreserved counsel, and for Yao and Shun, the only urgency was attending to the foremost duties. Why is this so? As for the foundations of the realm, nothing lies outside of family and state, soldiers and commoners; We wish to hear which among the supreme plans for them should come first, and which among the earnest hopes for them is most paramount. As for the manifestations of the ruler's mind, nothing is more evident than rites…

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
樂敎化朕欲聞其損益何
宜隆替何繫制治貴於未
亂其方術何良保邦貴於
未危其謀謨何遠以至為
政之寬猛何尚備邊之籌
===
策何長人才之賢否何由
刑賞之緩急何可與凡灾
祥感召之機何速夷狄向
背之故何在皆朕之所欲
聞者也夫事貴乎師古不
alt_text:
樂教化朕欲聞其損益何
宜隆替何繫制治貴於未
亂其方術何良保邦貴於
未危其謀謨何遠以至為
政之寬猛何尚備邊之籌
===
策何長人才之賢否何由
刑賞之緩急何可與凡災
祥感召之機何遠夷款向
背之故何在皆朕之所欲
聞者也夫事貴乎師古不
punctuated: 樂、敎化，朕欲聞其損益何宜，隆替何繫？制治貴於未亂，其方術何良？保邦貴於未危，其謀謨何遠？以至為政之寬猛何尚？備邊之籌策何長？人才之賢否何由？刑賞之緩急何可？與凡灾祥感召之機何速？夷狄向背之故何在？皆朕之所欲聞者也。夫事貴乎師古，不
translation_en: … [rites], music, and moral transformation: I wish to hear what additions and subtractions to them are appropriate, and upon what their flourishing or decline depends. Maintaining order is valued before disorder arises: what methods for this are best? Preserving the state is valued before danger strikes: what counsels for this are most far-reaching? Furthermore, in governance, how should leniency and severity be prioritized? In defending the frontiers, what strategic plans are superior? By what means are the worthiness and unworthiness of men of talent determined? What is the proper balance of urgency and restraint in punishments and rewards? And in general, why is the mechanism by which calamities and auspicious omens are evoked so swift? Wherein lies the reason for the submission or rebellion of foreign peoples? All of these are matters that I wish to hear about. Now, in affairs it is valuable to take antiquity as one's teacher; if one does not…

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
稽諸古固無足以為法於
今而施貴乎合宜不宜於
今又奚可以徒泥諸古子
大夫明先聖之道来應賓
興賢能之詔皆得於古而
===
將以施於今者也其悉叅
酌詳著于篇以俟朕之親
覽
alt_text:
稽諸古固無足以為法於
今而施貴乎合宜不宜於
今又奚可以徒泥諸古子
大夫明先聖之道來應賔
興賢能之詔皆得於古而
===
將以施於今者也其悉條
酌詳著于篇以俟朕之親
覽
punctuated: 稽諸古，固無足以為法於今；而施貴乎合宜，不宜於今，又奚可以徒泥諸古？子大夫明先聖之道，來應賓興賢能之詔，皆得於古而將以施於今者也。其悉叅酌，詳著于篇，以俟朕之親覽。
translation_en: …examined against antiquity, it is certainly insufficient to serve as a model for the present; yet in putting measures into practice, what is valued is suitability—if it is not suited to the present, how then can one merely cling blindly to antiquity? You gentlemen understand the Way of the former sages and have come in response to the imperial summons to honor and promote the worthy and capable; you have all acquired your learning from antiquity and are about to put it into practice in the present. Deliberate thoroughly on all these matters and set them forth in detail in your essays, awaiting Our personal perusal.

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
臣孫賢
臣對臣聞天生萬民必主以一人而後能任君
師之責君主萬民必運以一心而後能成治教
之功大哉人君之一心乎其萬化之原萬事之
本乎本諸心以治家國兵民則家國兵民無不
治本諸心以脩禮樂教化則禮樂教化無不脩
制治本諸心則制治之術良保邦本諸心則保
邦之謨遠以至為政備邊人材刑賞莫非以是
心為之本弭灾召祥綏懷夷狄莫非以是心為
之要孟子所謂家國天下之本董子所謂朝廷
===
四方之則是也恭惟
皇帝陛下稟聰明睿智之資備聖神文武之德誕膺
駿命茂續
鴻圖遠宗堯舜之道近守
祖宗之法道已臻皇極矣而猶惓惓顧惟負荷之艱
世已底雍煕矣而猶以為莫究弛張之善虛心
宵旰之是圖資弼忠良之是務乃進臣等于
廷降賜
明哲之問樂受盡言一至於此此誠大舜好問好
察大禹不自滿假成湯檢身若不及文王望道

臣對：臣聞天生萬民，必主以一人，而後能任君師之責；君主萬民，必運以一心，而後能成治教之功。大哉人君之一心乎！其萬化之原、萬事之本乎！本諸心以治家國兵民，則家國兵民無不治；本諸心以脩禮樂教化，則禮樂教化無不脩。制治本諸心，則制治之術良；保邦本諸心，則保邦之謨遠。以至為政、備邊、人材、刑賞，莫非以是心為之本；弭灾、召祥、綏懷夷狄，莫非以是心為之要。孟子所謂家國天下之本，董子所謂朝廷、四方之則，是也。恭惟皇帝陛下稟聰明睿智之資，備聖神文武之德，誕膺駿命，茂續鴻圖，遠宗堯、舜之道，近守祖宗之法。道已臻皇極矣，而猶惓惓顧惟負荷之艱；世已底雍煕矣，而猶以為莫究弛張之善。虛心宵旰之是圖，資弼忠良之是務。乃進臣等于廷，降賜明哲之問，樂受盡言一至於此。此誠大舜好問好察、大禹不自滿假、成湯檢身若不及、文王望道
translation_en:
Your servant Sun Xian 孫賢.

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that when Heaven gives birth to the myriad people, it must place one person in charge of them, and only then can the responsibilities of ruler and teacher be shouldered; when a ruler governs the myriad people, he must operate with a single mind, and only then can the achievements of governance and instruction be fulfilled. Great indeed is the single mind of the ruler! Is it not the source of all transformations and the root of all affairs? When he roots himself in this mind to govern family, state, military, and populace, then family, state, military, and populace are none of them ungoverned; when he roots himself in this mind to cultivate rites, music, and moral transformation, then rites, music, and moral transformation are none of them uncultivated. When establishing order is rooted in this mind, the methods of establishing order are sound; when preserving the state is rooted in this mind, the counsels for preserving the state are far-reaching. Extending even to administration, frontier defense, men of talent, and punishments and rewards, there is none that does not take this mind as its root; in averting disasters, summoning auspicious omens, and pacifying and winning over the border peoples, there is none that does not take this mind as its essential pivot. What Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) called the root of the family, the state, and All under Heaven, and what Master Dong (Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒) called the standard for the court and the four quarters—this is it.

Reverently I reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor is endowed with a disposition of keen perception and profound wisdom, and possesses the virtue of sagehood, divinity, civil accomplishment, and martial vigor. Greatly receiving the august mandate and flourishingly continuing the grand enterprise, You look afar to revere the Way of Yao 堯 and Shun 舜, and look near to uphold the laws of the Imperial Ancestors. Your Way has already reached the Supreme Ultimate, yet You still earnestly reflect on the difficulty of the burden You bear; the age has already attained harmonious prosperity, yet You still consider Yourself unable to exhaust the perfection of knowing when to relax and when to tighten governance. With an open mind, You devote Yourself to planning before dawn and eating only after dusk, and make it Your priority to rely on the assistance of the loyal and the good. Thus You have brought Your servants forward into the court, graciously bestowing Your sagacious questions, and taking delight in receiving unreserved counsel to such a degree as this. This truly is the magnificent mind of Great Shun, who loved to question and loved to examine; of Great Yu 禹, who was free from self-satisfaction and arrogance; of Tang the Successful 成湯, who examined himself as though he could never reach perfection; and of King Wen 文王, who looked toward the Way…

…as if he had not yet seen it. Your Majesty is truly a sovereign of great achievements, indeed a ruler who appears but once in an epoch; establishing the mind for Heaven and Earth, establishing the destiny for the living people, and inaugurating great peace for ten thousand generations—all rests squarely upon this! Yet considering how shallow and rustic your servant is, how could I be worthy of offering a grand reply? Still, how could I dare not exhaust my humble understanding, with a pure and single heart, in seeking to set forth my points so as to contribute even one part in ten thousand?

Your servant reflects that the great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life, and Yao and Shun treated first duties as urgent. When Your Majesty broadens the virtue of Heaven and Earth and models yourself on the governance of Yao and Shun, then in the enactment of every single policy and ordinance, what is not an expression of that great virtue and an urgent pursuit of the proper duty? The Classics say: "When the family is regulated, the state is rightly governed," and "When the root is firm, the country is tranquil." Therefore, the foundations of the empire lie nowhere outside of the family, the state, the military, and the people. Allow me to set forth the traces of how Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu managed family and state: What are called "being able to make illustrious his lofty virtue," "carefully cultivating his person," "being frugal in food and drink, and coarse in clothing," "staying far from seductive music and women, and not amassing goods and profit," "inquiring after comfort and inspecting the meals," and "illustrious virtue and far-reaching filial piety"—although these were the essentials by which the Two Emperors and Three Kings cultivated their persons, yet the person is the root of the family, and only when the person is cultivated is the family regulated; is not cultivating the person, then, the supreme plan for the family that ought to be put first? What are called "generously ordering the nine grades of kinsmen, and when the nine grades of kinsmen were harmonious," "being frugal in the family, and handing down abundance to later descendants," "main and collateral branches continuing in unbroken succession," and "fitting to be lord, fitting to be king"—although these were the essentials by which the Two Emperors and Three Kings regulated their families, yet the family is the root of the state, and only when the family is regulated is the state rightly governed; is not regulating the family, then, the supreme plan for the state that ought to be put first? text:
其備固兵之切望矣然必衣食有以養其體傜
役無以勞其形則兵切望之𠝹可副簡稼器備
稼政事乎農事使農有其備固民之切望矣然
必橫征暴斂有不加嚴刑峻法有不及則民切
望之𠝹可酬古之為將帥者與士卒同甘苦為
守令者愛百姓如己子所欲與聚所惡勿施而
已凡此何莫非兵民切望之𠝹乎古昔聖帝明
王慮民心之不中也制禮以防之而教之中憂
民情之不和也作樂以防之而教之和孔子嘗
言禮云禮云玉帛云乎哉樂云樂云鐘鼓云乎
===
哉盖謂玉帛有餘而敬不足則不足以為禮鐘
鼓有餘而和不足則不足以為樂必損有餘而
益不足則禮樂皆得其宜矣古者家有塾黨有
庠術有序國有學無一地而無學無一人而不
學人人有士君子之行比屋有可封之俗其教
化之所以隆者又豈無其故哉亦惟人君躬行
心得之餘言行政事皆可師法有以為之本耳
後世徒有興學之名而無興學之實此教化之
所以替也必以古人之躬行心得自勉而以後
世有名無實為戒則教化有隆無替矣自古畏

punctuated: 其備，固兵之切望矣。然必衣食有以養其體，傜役無以勞其形，則兵切望之𠝹可副。簡稼器，備稼政，事乎農事，使農有其備，固民之切望矣。然必橫征暴斂有不加，嚴刑峻法有不及，則民切望之𠝹可酬。古之為將帥者，與士卒同甘苦；為守令者，愛百姓如己子，所欲與聚，所惡勿施而已。凡此何莫非兵民切望之𠝹乎？古昔聖帝明王，慮民心之不中也，制禮以防之而教之中；憂民情之不和也，作樂以防之而教之和。孔子嘗言：「禮云禮云，玉帛云乎哉？樂云樂云，鐘鼓云乎哉？」盖謂玉帛有餘而敬不足，則不足以為禮；鐘鼓有餘而和不足，則不足以為樂。必損有餘而益不足，則禮樂皆得其宜矣。古者家有塾，黨有庠，術有序，國有學，無一地而無學，無一人而不學，人人有士君子之行，比屋有可封之俗，其教化之所以隆者，又豈無其故哉？亦惟人君躬行心得之餘，言行政事皆可師法，有以為之本耳。後世徒有興學之名，而無興學之實，此教化之所以替也。必以古人之躬行心得自勉，而以後世有名無實為戒，則教化有隆無替矣。自古畏
translation_en: … [make the troops have] their preparations, this is certainly the earnest wish of the troops. Yet only when food and clothing are sufficient to nourish their bodies, and corvée labor does not exhaust their frames, can the earnest wish of the troops be fulfilled. Selecting farming tools, preparing agricultural administration, and attending to farming matters so that agriculture has its preparations—this is certainly the earnest wish of the people. Yet only when arbitrary exactions and oppressive levies are not imposed, and severe punishments and harsh laws do not reach them, can the earnest wish of the people be satisfied. Those in antiquity who served as commanders and generals shared sweet and bitter with their soldiers; those who served as Grand Protectors and Magistrates loved the common people as their own children, simply gathering for them what they desired and not imposing upon them what they hated. Among all these things, what is not the earnest wish of the troops and the people? In ancient times, sage emperors and enlightened kings, concerned that the minds of the people were not balanced, instituted rites to restrain them and teach them balance; worried that the sentiments of the people were not harmonious, they created music to restrain them and teach them harmony. Confucius once said: "Rites, they say, rites! Does it mean no more than jade and silk? Music, they say, music! Does it mean no more than bells and drums?" This means that if there is an abundance of jade and silk but a deficiency of reverence, it is not enough to constitute rites; if there is an abundance of bells and drums but a deficiency of harmony, it is not enough to constitute music. Only when one diminishes what is excessive and supplements what is deficient will both rites and music attain their proper measure. In antiquity, families had family schools (shu), neighborhoods had neighborhood schools (xiang), districts had district schools (xu), and the state had the Imperial Academy (xue). There was not a single place without a school, nor a single person who did not study; everyone possessed the conduct of a scholar and a gentleman, and house after house had customs worthy of enfeoffment. Could there have been no reason why their moral transformation flourished so greatly? It was solely because, beyond the ruler's personal practice and inward attainment, his words, deeds, and governance could all serve as models to be emulated, thereby providing a foundation for it. Later ages merely had the name of promoting schools without the reality of promoting schools; this is why moral transformation declined. Only if one exhorts oneself with the personal practice and inward attainment of the ancients, and takes as a warning the nominal nature devoid of reality in later ages, will moral transformation flourish without decline. 危者必謹馭轡於康莊之途是以帝王之制治
也必於未亂之前若唐虞之君兢兢業業儆戒
無虞勅天之命惟時惟幾恒存此心於四方風
動之際此其方術可謂良矣故治已臻而益隆
帝王之保邦也必於未危之日若唐虞之君罔

江濤之險者，必慎舟楫於恬靜之頃；懼山蹊之危者，必謹馭轡於康莊之途。是以帝王之制治也，必於未亂之前。若唐虞之君，兢兢業業，儆戒無虞，勅天之命，惟時惟幾，恒存此心於四方風動之際，此其方術可謂良矣，故治已臻而益隆。帝王之保邦也，必於未危之日。若唐虞之君，罔遊于逸，罔淫于樂，任賢勿貳，去邪勿疑，恒率是道於萬邦咸寧之時，此其謀謨可謂遠矣，故邦愈寧而愈固。大抵銷危亂於未然者易為功，救危亂於已然者難為力。苟或事至而後圖之，患生而後弭之，雖有奇謀善術，未見其能濟也。
自古為政之道，貴於寬猛得宜。一於寬則流於姑息，而人無所懼；一於猛則入於苛刻，而下無所容。《詩》、《書》所稱「不剛不柔」、「輕重有權」，《周官》「刑新國用輕典，刑亂國用重典，刑平國用中典」，為政寬猛所尚，孰有過於此哉？備邊之策，在於守禦兼備。守不可以不固，不固則不足以安中國；禦不可以不嚴，不嚴則不足以攘夷狄。經傳所謂「維藩維翰」、「足食足兵」，《孟子》所謂「城非不高，池非不深，兵甲非不堅利」，備邊籌策之長，孰有要於是哉？
人才為政之首務。親賢臣，遠小人，

… the perils of river waves must take care with their boats and oars in moments of calm; those who dread the dangers of mountain paths must cautiously hold the reins on broad and level roads. Therefore, when emperors and kings establish order, they invariably do so before disorder arises. For instance, the rulers of Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun] were cautious and industrious, maintaining vigilance even when there was no cause for alarm, and respectfully fulfilling the Mandate of Heaven at every moment and in every subtle incipient sign. Because they constantly preserved this mindset even when all four quarters were moved by their transforming influence, their methods can truly be called excellent; thus, when good governance had already been achieved, it grew ever more flourishing. When emperors and kings preserve the state, they invariably do so on days before peril appears. For instance, the rulers of Tang and Yu did not wander in idleness or indulge in pleasure, employed the worthy without duplicity, and cast out the wicked without hesitation. Because they constantly followed this way even when the myriad states were all at peace, their counsels and plans can truly be called far-reaching; thus, the more peaceful the state became, the more secure it grew. In general, dispelling peril and disorder before they materialize is an easy way to achieve success, whereas rescuing a state from peril and disorder after they have already occurred requires difficult exertion. If one waits until trouble arrives before planning for it, or until disaster arises before quelling it, even with extraordinary counsels and fine methods, one will never see them succeed.

Since antiquity, the Way of governance has valued achieving the proper balance between leniency and severity. Exclusively relying on leniency degenerates into indulgence, leaving people with nothing to fear; exclusively relying on severity descends into harshness, leaving subordinates with no room to exist. What the Book of Odes (Shijing) and the Book of Documents (Shujing) refer to as being "neither too rigid nor too soft" and "weighing lightness and heaviness with discretion," and what the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan) states—"punish a newly established state with light statutes, punish a disorderly state with heavy statutes, and punish a peaceful state with moderate statutes"—regarding what should be esteemed in balancing leniency and severity in governance, what could surpass this? The strategy for frontier defense lies in preparing for both holding fortifications and repelling attacks. Defense cannot be anything less than solid, for if it is not solid, it is insufficient to bring security to the Central States; repelling attacks cannot be anything less than strict, for if it is not strict, it is insufficient to drive back the frontier tribes. What the classics and commentaries call acting as "a hedge and a bulwark" and having "sufficient food and sufficient soldiers," and what the Mencius (Mengzi) refers to as "walls not being lacking in height, moats not being lacking in depth, and weapons and armor not being lacking in solidity and sharpness"—among the superior plans and strategies for frontier defense, what could be more essential than these?

Men of talent are the foremost priority of governance. Drawing close to worthy ministers and keeping petty men at a distance…

text:
此先漢所以興隆也親小人遠賢士此後漢所
以傾頹也故凡有天下國家者惟在進賢而退
不肖盖賢者進則人莫不見賢而思齊不肖者
退則人皆見不肖而自省唐虞人才之盛本於
舜舉皋陶而誅四凶是其驗也此非人才賢否
之由而何刑賞人君之大權刑當其罪則刑一

輕功疑惟重罰弗及嗣賞延于世此非刑賞緩

translation_en:
… is why the Former Han flourished; keeping petty men close and holding worthygentlemen at a distance is why the Later Han declined and fell. Therefore, for all who possess the Empire and the state, everything lies solely in advancing the worthy and dismissing the unworthy. For when the worthy are advanced, there is no one who does not see the worthy and think of equaling them; when the unworthy are dismissed, everyone sees the unworthy and examines himself. The flourishing of men of talent under Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun] was rooted in Shun's raising up Gao Yao and executing the Four Criminals—this is the proof of it. What is this if not the reason why men of talent are worthy or unworthy?

Punishments and rewards are the great prerogative of the ruler of men. When punishment fits the crime, punishing one man makes ten million men fearful; when reward fits the merit, rewarding one man makes ten million men encouraged. Yet in the mind of the sage, approval of the good is prolonged while hatred of evil is brief. With Emperor Shun, in cases of doubtful guilt, punishment was lightened; in cases of doubtful merit, reward was made heavy; punishments did not extend to heirs, while rewards were carried on to later generations. What is this if not what is proper regarding urgency and leniency in punishments and rewards?

In the affairs of the world, whatever is manifested in human action has successes and failures, and therefore what appears in Heaven's response has calamities and auspicious omens. The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "The family that accumulates goodness is sure to have superabundant blessings; the family that accumulates evil is sure to have superabundant misfortune." The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Accordance with the right way brings good fortune; following the perverse brings misfortune"; and "On the doer of good, He sends down all blessings; on the doer of evil, He sends down all calamities"; and so on down to the favorable verifications responding to respectfulness, orderliness, wisdom, deliberation, and sageliness, and the unfavorable verifications responding to wildness, presumption, indolence, haste, and stolidity—all are examples of this. Now, good fortune and misfortune respond to good and evil just as shadow and echo issue from form and sound. Since it is like this, what could surpass the swiftness of the mechanism of stimulus and response? One cannot but be cautious about this!

The Yi and Di barbarians are not of our kindred race. Although they cannot be governed by the governance of the Central States, yet if there is a proper way to pacify and cherish them, then though they are utterly ignorant, they have a spiritual nature that can be moved and transformed. Bo Yi's admonition to Shun said: "Do not fail in the laws and ordinances; do not wander in idleness; do not go to excess in pleasure. Employ the worthy without duplicity; put away the wicked without hesitation; do not carry out doubtful plans. Do not go against the Way to seek the praise of the hundred surnames; …"

於乎！家國、兵民、禮樂、教化、制治、保邦、為政、備邊、人才、刑賞、灾祥、夷狄之事，此皆古昔聖帝明王之所已行，載諸經史，可以為訓者也。故傅說告高宗有曰：「學于古訓，乃有獲；事不師古，以克永世，匪說攸聞。」宜乎聖策有「事貴乎師古，不稽諸古，無以為法於今」之諭，此臣固有以知陛下之心，即古昔帝王之盛心矣。然而時異勢殊，宜於古者或有不合於今，膠柱調瑟、刻舟求劒，在古人深以為戒；精一執中、因時制宜，雖聖智所不能違。宜乎聖策有「施貴乎合宜，不宜於今，豈可徒泥諸古」之訓，此臣又有以知陛下之心，即權衡萬化之盛心也。所謂「大哉心乎，萬化之原，萬事之本」者，此也。陛下誠運是心以齊家、治國、詰兵、養民，則家齊、國治、
translation_en:
… do not oppose the common people to follow your own desires; without negligence and without indulgence, the barbarian tribes of the four quarters will come to acknowledge your sovereignty"; and Duke Shao's admonition to King Cheng (Chengwang 成王): "When an enlightened king carefully attends to his virtue, the barbarian tribes of the four quarters all come as guests; when he does not prize things from afar, then people from afar will come"—examples such as these are what is meant. Viewed in this light, in how emperors and kings deal with the non-Chinese tribes, if they act in accordance with this principle, the tribes submit; if they act contrary to it, the tribes depart. This being so, how could the reasons for their allegiance or defection lie anywhere outside of this?

Alas! The affairs of family and state, soldiers and civilians, rites and music, moral transformation through education, establishing order and preserving the state, conducting government and defending the frontiers, men of talent, punishments and rewards, calamities and auspicious omens, and the non-Chinese tribes—all of these are what the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity have already practiced, and what is recorded in the Classics and Histories to serve as instruction. Therefore, Fu Yue 傅說 told King Gaozong 高宗: "One should learn from the lessons of antiquity, and then one will achieve results. That affairs not modeled on antiquity can endure for generations is something Yue has not heard of." Fitting indeed is the pronouncement in Your Majesty's policy question that "in affairs, the essential thing is to take antiquity as one's teacher; without examining antiquity, there is no way to establish models for the present." From this, your servant truly has the means to know that Your Majesty's mind is none other than theflourishing mind of the emperors and kings of antiquity. Yet times change and circumstances differ; what was suitable in antiquity may sometimes not accord with the present. Tuning a zither with glued pegs and carving a mark on a boat to look for a dropped sword were things against which the ancients deeply warned. Being discerning and undivided to hold fast the Mean, and instituting what is appropriate according to the times—even sage wisdom cannot depart from this. Fitting indeed is the instruction in Your Majesty's policy question that "in implementation, the essential thing is to accord with what is appropriate; if it is not suitable for the present, how can one merely cling obstinately to antiquity?" From this, your servant further has the means to know that Your Majesty's mind is none other than the flourishing mind that weighs and balances the myriad transformations. This is what is meant by "Great indeed is the mind, the source of the myriad transformations and the root of the myriad affairs!" If Your Majesty truly applies this mind to regulate the family, govern the state, drill the troops, and nourish the people, then the family will be regulated, the state will be governed, …

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
而兵備民安誠運是心以制禮作樂敦行教化
則禮備樂和而化行俗美以至制治保邦為政
備邊非運是心不足以成其功人才刑賞灾祥
夷狄非運是心不足以臻其效然則天下之事
惟貴於得其要不得其要則事雖簡治以眾人
而不足苟得其要則事雖繁運以一心而有餘
此臣所為惓惓以運是心為
陛下陳之也
陛下之策臣者臣既以此陳之而於終篇竊有獻焉
何也天地無心而成化聖人有心而無為天地
===
無心而覆載萬物無遺者以其至誠無息所致
也聖人有心而酬酢萬化無失者以其純亦不
已所使也臣願
陛下體天地之無息運酬酢之盛心始終惟一宵旰
無間則遠追配乎二帝三王近光昭乎
祖宗列聖無難矣臣學不足以明先聖之道才不足
以適當今之宜芻蕘之言上塵
聖覽伏惟
陛下少垂采納則
國家幸甚天下幸甚臣不勝悚懼之至臣謹對

punctuated:
而兵備民安。誠運是心以制禮作樂、敦行教化，則禮備樂和，而化行俗美。以至制治保邦、為政備邊，非運是心不足以成其功；人才刑賞、灾祥夷狄，非運是心不足以臻其效。然則天下之事，惟貴於得其要。不得其要，則事雖簡，治以眾人而不足；苟得其要，則事雖繁，運以一心而有餘。此臣所為惓惓以運是心為陛下陳之也。
陛下之策臣者，臣既以此陳之，而於終篇竊有獻焉。何也？天地無心而成化，聖人有心而無為。天地無心，而覆載萬物無遺者，以其至誠無息所致也；聖人有心，而酬酢萬化無失者，以其純亦不已所使也。臣願陛下體天地之無息，運酬酢之盛心，始終惟一，宵旰無間，則遠追配乎二帝三王，近光昭乎祖宗列聖，無難矣。
臣學不足以明先聖之道，才不足以適當今之宜，芻蕘之言，上塵聖覽。伏惟陛下少垂采納，則國家幸甚，天下幸甚。臣不勝悚懼之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…the army will be well-prepared, and the people will be at peace. Truly, if You employ this mind to institute rites and compose music, and to earnestly promote moral transformation, then rites will be complete and music harmonious, moral transformation will prevail, and customs will be noble. Extending even to establishing order and securing the state, administering government and defending the frontiers—without employing this mind, it is impossible to achieve their success; and regarding men of talent, punishments and rewards, portents of disaster and auspice, and the border tribes—without employing this mind, it is impossible to attain their efficacy. This being so, in all affairs under Heaven, the only thing to be valued is grasping their essential point. If one does not grasp their essential point, then even though affairs be simple, governing them with a multitude of people will not suffice; if one does grasp their essential point, then even though affairs be manifold, managing them with a single mind will leave capacity to spare. This is why your servant so earnestly sets forth the employment of this mind for Your Majesty.

As for the policy questions Your Majesty has posed to your servant, having already set forth my answers in this manner, at the close of this essay I humbly venture to offer a further word. Why is this? Heaven and Earth have no deliberate mind, yet they bring about transformations; the sage has a deliberate mind, yet acts through non-purposive action. That Heaven and Earth have no deliberate mind and yet shelter and sustain the myriad things without omission is brought about by their utmost sincerity without cease; that the sage has a deliberate mind and yet responds to the myriad transformations without error is caused by his unmixed purity that likewise never stops. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty embody the unceasing nature of Heaven and Earth and employ a flourishing mind that responds to all things, remaining unified from beginning to end and allowing no pause from before dawn until after dark; then to match the Two Emperors and Three Kings in the distant past, and to gloriously manifest our Ancestors and Successive Sage-Emperors in recent times, will present no difficulty at all.

Your servant's learning is insufficient to illuminate the Way of the former sages, and my talent is insufficient to meet the needs of the present day; the words of a mere grass-cutter and firewood-gatherer rise to soil Your Sacred Glance. Prostrate, I pray that Your Majesty may deign to accept and adopt a small part of them; then the State will be most fortunate, and all under Heaven will be most fortunate. Your servant is overcome with the utmost trepidation and awe. Your servant respectfully replies.

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
臣徐溥
臣對臣聞聖人之治本於道聖人之道本於心
盖心者萬化之原萬事之本也堯舜以是心而
帝天下三王以是心而王天下惟其道本於心
故聖人之道備惟其治本於道故聖人之治隆

臣徐溥。
臣對：臣聞聖人之治，本於道；聖人之道，本於心。盖心者，萬化之原，萬事之本也。堯、舜以是心而帝天下，三王以是心而王天下。惟其道本於心，故聖人之道備；惟其治本於道，故聖人之治隆。故凡欲求聖人之治者，不可不求其道；欲求聖人之道者，不可不求其心。董仲舒所謂「正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官，正百官以正萬民，正萬民以正四方」，即此意也。欽惟皇帝陛下，聰明睿智，足以有臨；聖神文武，自強不息。紹祖德而誕膺天命，應人心而中興邦家。勤勵以親萬幾，惇慎以弘萬化。純孝之德，播聞於宇宙之間；仁厚之澤，漸被於覆幬之下。然猶慮負荷之艱，而欲究弛張之善，乃進臣等于廷，降賜清問。臣有以知陛下是心，即堯、舜稽于衆、好察邇言之心，湯、文用人
translation_en:
Your servant Xu Pu 徐溥.
Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that the governance of the sages is rooted in the Way, and the Way of the sages is rooted in the mind. For the mind is the source of the myriad transformations and the foundation of the myriad affairs. With this mind, Yao 堯 and Shun 舜 ruled All under Heaven as emperors; with this mind, the Three Kings ruled All under Heaven as kings. Because their Way was rooted in the mind, the Way of the sages was complete; because their governance was rooted in the Way, the governance of the sages flourished. Therefore, anyone who wishes to seek the governance of the sages cannot but seek their Way; anyone who wishes to seek the Way of the sages cannot but seek their mind. What Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒 meant by "rectifying the mind in order to rectify the court, rectifying the court in order to rectify the hundred officials, rectifying the hundred officials in order to rectify the myriad people, and rectifying the myriad people in order to rectify the four quarters" is precisely this idea. Reverently, I reflect that Your Imperial Majesty is sagacious, discerning, and wise enough to rule over all; sacred, divine, civil, and martial, ceaselessly strengthening yourself. Succeeding to the virtue of your Ancestors, you have grandly received the Mandate of Heaven; responding to the minds of the people, you have brought about a restoration of the state. With diligence and exertion you personally attend to the myriad affairs of state; with sincerity and prudence you broaden the myriad transformations. The virtue of your pure filiality is proclaimed and heard throughout the universe; the grace of your benevolence and generosity gradually reaches everywhere under the canopy of Heaven and Earth. Yet, still mindful of the difficulty of bearing this great burden and wishing to thoroughly investigate the best principles of relaxing and tightening governance, you have summoned your servants to the court and condescended to bestow your exalted inquiry. Your servant thereby knows that this mind of Your Majesty is none other than the mind of Yao and Shun in consulting the multitude and delighting in examining near words, and the flourishing mind of Tang 湯 and King Wen 文王 in employing others…

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
惟已望道未見之盛心也其復隆古之至治而
開萬世之太平端在於此顧臣愚昧何足以奉
大對然敢不精白一心以對揚
陛下之明命乎請因
聖問所及而條陳之竊以家者一國之所視效國者
天下之所取法而兵民又所以衛民生而固邦
本者也
陛下於齊家治國之道練兵安民之方皆已行之有
其效矣茲猶欲聞至計何先切望何最臣願
陛下正心以為家國兵民之本而祖述於唐虞三代
===
之迹正倫理篤恩義如堯之親睦九族道以德
齊以禮如堯之平章百姓則九族既睦百姓昭
明而家可齊國可治矣修車馬備器械而時其
簡教如成周之治兵大閱有定制制田里薄賦
斂以給其衣食如成周之分田制賦有常法則
兵農相資守養相益而用可利生可厚矣若夫
安上治民莫善於禮移風易俗莫善於樂而教
化又所以復民性而正民德者也
陛下於制禮作樂之方敷教弘化之道皆已行之有
其驗矣茲猶欲聞損益所宜隆替所係臣願

惟已、望道未見之盛心也。其復隆古之至治，而開萬世之太平，端在於此。顧臣愚昧，何足以奉大對？然敢不精白一心，以對揚陛下之明命乎！請因聖問所及而條陳之。

竊以家者，一國之所視效；國者，天下之所取法；而兵民又所以衛民生而固邦本者也。陛下於齊家治國之道、練兵安民之方，皆已行之有其效矣，茲猶欲聞至計何先、切望何最。臣願陛下正心以為家國兵民之本，而祖述於唐、虞、三代之迹。正倫理、篤恩義，如堯之親睦九族；道以德、齊以禮，如堯之平章百姓，則九族既睦，百姓昭明，而家可齊、國可治矣。修車馬、備器械，而時其簡教，如成周之治兵大閱有定制；制田里、薄賦斂，以給其衣食，如成周之分田制賦有常法，則兵農相資，守養相益，而用可利、生可厚矣。

若夫安上治民，莫善於禮；移風易俗，莫善於樂；而教化又所以復民性而正民德者也。陛下於制禮作樂之方、敷教弘化之道，皆已行之有其驗矣，茲猶欲聞損益所宜、隆替所係。臣願…
translation_en:
…employing others as if their merits were one's own and looking toward the Way as though not yet seeing it. Restoring the supreme governance of high antiquity and inaugurating peace for ten thousand generations truly lies herein. Yet as your servant is foolish and unenlightened, how could I be worthy of offering a grand reply? Even so, how could I dare not keep a pure and single heart in answering and extolling Your Majesty's illustrious command! Allow me to set forth my points in order according to what the sacred inquiry has touched upon.

I humbly submit that the family is what an entire state looks to and emulates, the state is what the entire realm takes as its model, and soldiers and the common people are the means by which the people's livelihood is defended and the foundation of the realm is secured. With regard to the Way of regulating the family and governing the state, and the methods of training soldiers and bringing peace to the people, Your Majesty has already put them all into practice with effective results; yet now You still wish to hear what supreme plan comes first and what urgent expectation is paramount. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty rectify Your mind to serve as the foundation of family, state, soldiers, and people, while following the footsteps of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. By rectifying human relationships and deepening kindness and righteousness, just as Yao brought harmony to the nine branches of the kin; and by guiding them with virtue and regulating them with rites, just as Yao brought order and distinction to the hundred surnames—when the nine branches of the kin are harmonious and the hundred surnames are enlightened, the family can be regulated and the state can be governed. By repairing chariots and horses, preparing weapons and equipment, and conducting timely inspections and drills, just as the flourishing Zhou had fixed institutions for military training and grand reviews; and by regulating fields and residences and lightening taxes and levies to supply their clothing and food, just as the flourishing Zhou had constant laws for allotting fields and regulating military levies—when soldiery and agriculture support each other and defense and nourishment mutually benefit one another, instruments can be made effective and livelihoods can be enriched.

As for securing superiors and governing the people, nothing is better than rites; for transforming customs and changing habits, nothing is better than music; and moral instruction and transformation are the means by which the people's nature is restored and the people's virtue is rectified. With regard to the methods of instituting rites and creating music, and the Way of spreading instruction and broadening transformation, Your Majesty has already put them all into practice with proven results; yet now You still wish to hear what additions and subtractions are appropriate and upon what their flourishing and decline depend. Your servant wishes…

If those in charge of rites are like Boyi, who was "reverent morning and night, upright and pure," and those in charge of music are like Lord Kui, under whom "the eight musical tones were harmonious and did not encroach upon one another's order," then additions and subtractions will hit the proper mean, and rites will be complete and music harmonious. …nor mild, he spreads his governance gently and generously." These are the fine methods by which the sages pacified the world, responded to affairs, and instituted measures suited to the times. If Your Majesty truly acts as praised in the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu), tempering leniency with severity and complementing firmness with gentleness, then using the yang principle to expand and the yin principle to restrain, You will grasp both extremes and employ the mean among the people.

The Book of Documents says: "Five hundred li constitute the Pacified Zone: in the first three hundred li they regulate civil instruction; in the outer two hundred li they exert military defense." The civil is used to govern the interior, and the martial is used to control the exterior. The Book of Odes says: "We attack the Xianyun and fortify that northern region." This is the essential way by which the sages brought peace to China, repelled the barbarians, and prudently secured the frontiers. If Your Majesty truly acts as recorded in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, cultivating civil virtue within and tightening military preparedness without—stationing troops for defense, attending to agriculture for food, raising high walls and strong ramparts—then You will be able to repulse external insults.

When superior men are employed, they advance their state into glorious enlightenment; when petty men are employed, they plunge their state into dark obscurity. The criteria distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy among men of talent truly cannot go unknown. Your Majesty has repeatedly issued edicts to the court and provinces to promote the worthy and dismiss the degenerate, yet now You still wish to hear the criteria distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy. Your servant wishes Your Majesty to rectify Your mind as the standard of impartiality in promotions and dismissals, ensuring that the worthy are unfailingly promoted and the degenerate unfailingly dismissed. Just as Confucius said, "Promote the upright and set aside the crooked," then the path of selfish scrambling for advancement will be blocked, men of the nine virtues will all be in service, and no worthy man will be left overlooked in the wilderness.

Rewards must be bestowed upon superior men before the people are encouraged; punishments must be inflicted upon petty men before the people are awed. What is appropriate regarding urgency and leniency in punishments and rewards truly must be carefully examined. Your Majesty has repeatedly admonished the various offices to be strict in bestowing ranks, rewards, and punishments, yet now You still wish to hear what is appropriate regarding urgency and leniency. Your servant wishes…

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
陛下正心以為勸懲之本有罪者必刑有德者必賞
如虞書所謂黜幽而陟明則僥倖之心沮百工
惟時庶績咸熈矣人事有得失而災祥不能無
徵應也
陛下誠省身脩德敬天勤民於上羣臣咸盡忠竭力
奉法脩職於下則雨暘順而百穀登禍亂銷而
千災殄矣時政有治忽夷狄不能無窺伺也
陛下誠賤貨貴德愛民好士為之本諸臣咸攄誠宣
威練兵鼓勇為之用則信義立而強梗化夷狄
賓而蠻戎服矣凡此數者何莫而非本於
===
陛下一心之運用乎夫心固為致治之本而古又為
致治之法傅說所謂事不師古以克永世匪說
攸聞孟子所謂為高必因丘陵為下必因川澤
為政必因先王之道是也若使徒稽諸古而不
以施於事則為徒善不足以為政徒泥諸古而
有不宜於今則為徒法不能以自行故必益之
損之與時宜之如中庸所謂時措之宜乃可也
陛下之策臣者臣既畧陳之矣臣於終篇竊有獻焉
臣惟天地之所以能成歲功者以其常運之不
已也帝王之所以能成治功者以其常德之不

… Your Majesty rectifies his mind to serve as the foundation for encouragement and chastisement, ensuring that those with offenses are inevitably punished and those with virtue are inevitably rewarded—just as the Book of Yu (Yushu) speaks of "demoting thedark and promoting the bright"—then opportunistic thoughts will be thwarted, all officials will act in accordance with the seasons, and all achievements will flourish. Human affairs have successes and failures, and calamities and auspicious omens cannot fail to manifest in response. If Your Majesty truly examines himself, cultivates virtue, reveres Heaven, and labors diligently for the people above, while the assembled ministers all exhaust their loyalty and strength, uphold the laws, and fulfill their duties below, then rain and sunshine will be timely and the hundred grains will yield abundantly, disasters and disorders will dissolve, and a thousand calamities will be eradicated. Current governance has periods of order and neglect, and the border tribes cannot fail to spy for opportunities. If Your Majesty truly disdains material goods and values virtue, loving the people and cherishing scholars as the foundation, while the various ministers all pour forth their sincerity and project majesty, training troops and rousing courage as the practical application, then trustworthiness and righteousness will be established and the recalcitrant will be transformed, the border tribes will submit as guests, and the southern Man and western Rong peoples will be pacified. Among all these several matters, which of them does not fundamentally stem from the operation of Your Majesty's single mind?

Now, the mind is assuredly the foundation for achieving good order, while antiquity serves in turn as the model for achieving good order. This is what Fu Yue meant in saying, "That in affairs one could refrain from taking antiquity as a teacher and yet be able to perpetuate one's generation is something Yue has not heard of," and what Mencius (Mengzi) meant in saying, "To build high one must make use of hills and mounds; to dig deep one must make use of streams and marshes; to govern one must make use of the Way of the Former Kings." Yet if one merely investigates antiquity without applying it to practical affairs, that is what is meant by "mere goodness is insufficient for governing"; and if one merely clings rigidly to antiquity when it is unsuitable for the present, that is what is meant by "mere laws cannot put themselves into practice." Therefore, one must add to it and subtract from it, adapting it appropriately to the times; only when it accords with what the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) calls "the appropriateness of timely application" will it suffice.

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
聖德配天地明同日月誠又存持久之心秉有常
之德則何所往而不宜哉書曰常厥德保厥位
將見四三王而六五帝參天地而贊化育曆數
衍億萬斯年之久聲名施中國蠻貊之遥皆在
於此尚何負荷之艱之足慮哉臣荷蒙
教育之恩來應賓興之詔學不足以博古識不足
以通今誤辱
九重之清問獻以一得之愚思干冒
天聰不勝怖懼臣謹對

punctuated: 聖德配天地，明同日月，誠又存持久之心，秉有常之德，則何所往而不宜哉！《書》曰：「常厥德，保厥位。」將見四三王而六五帝，參天地而贊化育，曆數衍億萬斯年之久，聲名施中國蠻貊之遥，皆在於此，尚何負荷之艱之足慮哉！臣荷蒙教育之恩，來應賓興之詔，學不足以博古，識不足以通今，誤辱九重之清問，獻以一得之愚思。干冒天聰，不勝怖懼。臣謹對。
translation_en: …Your Majesty's sacred virtue matches Heaven and Earth, and Your brilliance equals the sun and the moon. If You truly also preserve an enduring mind and uphold a constant virtue, then wherever You turn, what will not be fitting! The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Be constant in your virtue to preserve your throne." We shall soon see You stand as a fourth to the Three Kings and a sixth to the Five Emperors, form a triad with Heaven and Earth and assist in their transforming and nourishing work, extend the dynastic destiny through myriad years of longevity, and spread Your renown afar throughout the Central States and the barbarian tribes—all of this rests right here. How then could the difficulty of bearing the great burden still be cause for concern! Your servant, having received the grace of imperial education, has come in response to the edict summoning worthy guests. My learning is insufficient to encompass antiquity, and my insight is insufficient to comprehend the present. Having unworthily been graced by the pure inquiry from the Ninefold Palace, I offer the humble thoughts of my single modest attainment. Offending Your Heavenly hearing, I am overcome with fear and trembling. Your servant respectfully replies.

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄

臣徐轄
臣對臣聞天下之本在於一人人君之本在於
一心聖人不以天下視天下而以一心域天下
以天下視天下則天下至大而無外以一心域
天下則天下雖大而可容故三皇以道治天下
者此心也五帝以德化天下者此心也三王以
功率天下者庸有出於此心之外哉由是而知
家國之至計兵民之切望在乎此心之運行禮
樂之損益教化之隆替在乎此心之存否心乎
惟幾惟康則致治保邦其方術謨謀之良且遠
===
可得心乎隨時制宜則為政備邊其寬猛籌策
所尚所長可求以至人才賢否之由刑賞緩急
之當灾祥感召之機夷狄向背之故何莫不自
人君一心中來耶大哉心乎其為人君天下之
所倚賴者乎欽惟
皇帝陛下聰明睿智剛健齊莊體帝王致治之要道
法
祖宗贊化之宏規治已至而恒若未至化已隆而恒
若未隆乃進臣等於
廷降賜

臣對：臣聞天下之本在於一人，人君之本在於一心。聖人不以天下視天下，而以一心域天下。以天下視天下，則天下至大而無外；以一心域天下，則天下雖大而可容。故三皇以道治天下者，此心也；五帝以德化天下者，此心也；三王以功率天下者，庸有出於此心之外哉？由是而知家國之至計、兵民之切望，在乎此心之運行；禮樂之損益、教化之隆替，在乎此心之存否。心乎惟幾惟康，則致治保邦，其方術謨謀之良且遠可得；心乎隨時制宜，則為政備邊，其寬猛籌策所尚所長可求。以至人才賢否之由、刑賞緩急之當、灾祥感召之機、夷狄向背之故，何莫不自人君一心中來耶？大哉心乎！其為人君天下之所倚賴者乎！欽惟皇帝陛下，聰明睿智，剛健齊莊，體帝王致治之要道，法祖宗贊化之宏規，治已至而恒若未至，化已隆而恒若未隆，乃進臣等於廷，降賜
translation_en:
Your servant Xu Xia 徐轄.

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that the foundation of all under Heaven lies in the One Man, and the foundation of the ruler of men lies in the one mind. The sage does not view all under Heaven by means of all under Heaven, but encompasses all under Heaven by means of the one mind. If one views all under Heaven by means of all under Heaven, then all under Heaven is vast beyond bounds; if one encompasses all under Heaven by means of the one mind, then although all under Heaven is vast, it can be contained. Therefore, that by which the Three Sovereigns governed all under Heaven with the Way was this mind; that by which the Five Emperors transformed all under Heaven with virtue was this mind; and as for that by which the Three Kings led all under Heaven with achievements—how could it ever go beyond this mind? From this we know that the supreme plans for state and family, and the earnest hopes of soldiers and civilians, depend upon the operation of this mind; the additions and subtractions to rites and music, and the flourishing and decline of moral transformation, depend upon whether this mind is preserved or not. When the mind attends to the subtle incipient springs of things and to stability, then in bringing about order and preserving the state, the excellence and far-reaching nature of its methods and counsels can be attained; when the mind adapts to the times and establishes what is appropriate, then in administering government and preparing the frontiers, what is valued and what excels in its strategies of leniency and severity can be sought. Extending even to the reasons for the worthiness or unworthiness of men of talent, the proper balance of urgency and deliberation in punishments and rewards, the mechanisms by which calamities and auspicious omens are called forth, and the causes for the allegiance or defection of barbarian tribes—which of these does not arise from within the one mind of the ruler of men? Great indeed is the mind! Is it not that upon which the ruler of men and all under Heaven rely? Reverently I reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor, intelligent and wise, vigorous and grave, embodies the essential Way by which the emperors and kings brought about order, and models himself on the grand regulations by which the Ancestors assisted cosmic transformation. Order has already reached its utmost, yet You ever act as though it had not yet been reached; transformation is already flourishing, yet You ever act as though it were not yet flourishing. Thus You have brought Your servants forward into the court and handed down…

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
清問臣雖草茅微陋敢不稽首頓首以對揚
聖天子之休命乎臣聞
陛下天性聰明嗣
祖宗之大業盡君道之難矣而猶顧惟負荷之艱行
帝王之大事得執中之道矣猶謂莫究弛張之
善乃虛心於宵旰冀資弼於忠良臣有以知
陛下不自滿假之心真可以四三王而六五帝不屑
小康之意真可以光
先烈而垂後昆
國家幸甚天下幸甚臣聞閨門之內萬化出焉朝
===
廷之上四方效焉國以民為本民以兵為衛誠
如
聖策所謂天下之本莫有外於家國兵民者也
陛下內盡親親之道外施平章之化家齊而國治矣
猶欲聞其至計何先被堅執銳者閑於禦衛出
作入息者安於教養兵備而民安矣猶欲聞其
切望何最誠以親睦九族平章百姓惇敘九族
庶明勵翼堯舜之齊家治國也而孰知其本於
克明俊德身脩思永曰明德曰思永非堯舜家
國之至計所當先乎臣願

臣聞陛下天性聰明，嗣祖宗之大業，盡君道之難矣，而猶顧惟負荷之艱；行帝王之大事，得執中之道矣，猶謂莫究弛張之善。乃虛心於宵旰，冀資弼於忠良。臣有以知陛下不自滿假之心，真可以四三王而六五帝；不屑小康之意，真可以光先烈而垂後昆。國家幸甚！天下幸甚！
臣聞閨門之內，萬化出焉；朝廷之上，四方效焉。國以民為本，民以兵為衛，誠如聖策所謂天下之本莫有外於家、國、兵、民者也。陛下內盡親親之道，外施平章之化，家齊而國治矣，猶欲聞其至計何先；被堅執銳者閑於禦衛，出作入息者安於教養，兵備而民安矣，猶欲聞其切望何最。誠以親睦九族，平章百姓，惇敘九族，庶明勵翼，堯、舜之齊家治國也，而孰知其本於克明俊德、身脩思永？曰「明德」、曰「思永」，非堯、舜家國之至計所當先乎？臣願
translation_en:
… gracious inquiry. Although your servant is a humble rustic from the thatched cottages, how dare he not bow his head to the ground to respond to and extol theSacred Son of Heaven's illustrious mandate!

Your servant hears that Your Majesty, endowed by heaven with intelligence and wisdom, has succeeded to the great enterprise of the Imperial Ancestors. You have fulfilled the difficult duties of the way of the ruler, yet still reflect upon the hardship of bearing this heavy burden; you have carried out the great affairs of emperors and kings and attained the way of holding fast the Mean, yet still say you have not exhausted the perfection of knowing when to relax and when to tighten. Thus you humble your mind through late nights and late meals, hoping to rely on the assistance of the loyal and good. From this your servant knows that Your Majesty's mind, never self-satisfied or arrogant, can truly make a fourth to the Three Kings and a sixth to the Five Emperors; your intention, disdaining mere Lesser Tranquility, can truly bring glory to the achievements of your predecessors and hand down a legacy to future descendants. Most fortunate for the dynasty! Most fortunate for All under Heaven!

Your servant has heard that from within the inner quarters of the palace, the myriad transformations issue forth; from above in the imperial court, the four quarters take their model. The state takes the people as its foundation, and the people take the military as their defense—truly as Your Majesty's sacred policy question states, the foundation of All under Heaven lies in nothing outside of the family, the state, the military, and the people. Your Majesty internally fulfills the way of affection toward kin and externally extends the transforming influence of harmonious governance; the family is regulated and the state is rightly governed, yet you still wish to hear what supreme plan should come first. Those who wear armor and wield sharp weapons are well-trained in defense and protection, and those who go out to work at sunrise and return to rest at sunset are content in their instruction and nourishment; military preparedness is complete and the people are at peace, yet you still wish to hear what urgent expectation is most paramount. Indeed, bringing harmony to the nine grades of kinsmen and regulating the hundred surnames, generously ordering the nine grades of kinsmen so that thenumerous enlightened officials exert themselves as wings of assistance—this was how Yao and Shun regulated the family and governed the state. Yet who knows that it was rooted in being able to make illustrious their lofty virtue, and in cultivating the person while thinking of perpetuity? What are called "illustrious virtue" and "thinking of perpetuity"—are these not what should come first in the supreme plan of Yao and Shun for family and state? Your servant wishes that …

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
陛下推是心以脩身齊家則家齊而國治矣比其什
伍時其簡敎成周之治兵也而實本於共武之
服者之有嚴有翼契敷五敎稷播百穀唐虞之
理民也而實本於臨下御衆者之以簡以寛曰
嚴翼曰簡寛非虞周兵民之切望爲獨最乎臣
願
陛下推是心以詰兵養民則兵備而民安矣禮非止
於儀章度數而實本於心之敬樂非止於五音
六律而實本於心之和必資躬行心得之餘斯
致化行俗美之效誠如
===
聖策所謂君心之發莫有著於禮樂敎化者也
陛下治定制禮功成作樂禮樂固已明備矣猶欲聞
其損益何宜敎立於上化行於下敎化固已美
盛矣猶欲聞其隆替何繫臣聞上衣下裳之有
制大章大韶之有作堯舜之禮樂也原其制作
之本則在命伯夷之寅清命后夔之直溫曰寅
清曰直溫堯舜不外乎此心也臣願
陛下以是心爲制作之本益之損之與時宜之參以
兒寛所謂兼總條貫金聲玉振則損益得其宜
矣江沱從化汝墳遵敎文王之敎化也而實本

陛下推是心以脩身齊家，則家齊而國治矣。比其什伍，時其簡敎，成周之治兵也，而實本於共武之服者之有嚴有翼；契敷五敎，稷播百穀，唐虞之理民也，而實本於臨下御衆者之以簡以寛。曰嚴翼，曰簡寛，非虞周兵民之切望爲獨最乎？臣願陛下推是心以詰兵養民，則兵備而民安矣。

禮非止於儀章度數，而實本於心之敬；樂非止於五音六律，而實本於心之和。必資躬行心得之餘，斯致化行俗美之效。誠如聖策所謂君心之發莫有著於禮樂敎化者也。陛下治定制禮，功成作樂，禮樂固已明備矣，猶欲聞其損益何宜；敎立於上，化行於下，敎化固已美盛矣，猶欲聞其隆替何繫。臣聞上衣下裳之有制，大章、大韶之有作，堯、舜之禮樂也，原其制作之本，則在命伯夷之寅清，命后夔之直溫。曰寅清，曰直溫，堯、舜不外乎此心也。臣願陛下以是心爲制作之本，益之損之，與時宜之，參以兒寛所謂「兼總條貫，金聲玉振」，則損益得其宜矣。江沱從化，汝墳遵敎，文王之敎化也，而實本
translation_en:
… Your Majesty extend this mind to cultivate your person and regulate your family, and then the family will be regulated and the state rightly governed. Organizing the troops into squads of five and ten and conducting their inspection and training at the proper seasons was how the Zhou in its heyday governed the military, yet in truth this was rooted in the solemnity and reverence of him who discharged the martial duties. Xie propagating the five teachings and Hou Ji sowing the hundred grains was how Tang and Yu governed the people, yet in truth this was rooted in the simplicity and leniency of him who presided over his subjects and ruled the multitude. What are called "solemnity and reverence" and "simplicity and leniency"—were these not preeminently the most earnest aspirations for the military and the people under Yu and Zhou? Your servant wishes that Your Majesty extend this mind to scrutinize the military and nourish the people, and then military preparedness will be maintained and the people will be at peace.

Ritual does not stop at ceremonial insignia and graded measures, but is truly rooted in the reverence of the mind; music does not stop at the five tones and six pitch-pipes, but is truly rooted in the harmony of the mind. Only by relying on the abundance of personal practice and inner attainment can one bring about the effect of moral transformation spreading and customs becoming beautiful. It is truly as Your Majesty's sacred policy question states: "Nothing in the manifestation of the ruler's mind is more evident than ritual, music, and moral teaching and transformation." Your Majesty has instituted rituals once governance was settled, and created music once achievements were completed; ritual and music are indeed already clear and complete, yet You still wish to hear what is appropriate in adding to or subtracting from them. Teaching is established above, and transformation is carried out below; moral teaching and transformation are indeed already admirable and flourishing, yet You still wish to hear upon what their rise and decline depend. Your servant has heard that the system of upper garments and lower skirts, and the composition of the Dazhang and Dashao music, were the ritual and music of Yao and Shun. Tracing the foundation of their creation, it lay in charging Boyi with reverence and purity, and charging Hou Kui with uprightness and mildness. What are called "reverence and purity" and "uprightness and mildness"—Yao and Shun did not go beyond this mind. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty take this mind as the foundation of creation, adding to them and subtracting from them to suit the times, and consult what Ni Kuan 兒寬 called "comprehending and uniting the threads of principle, like the sounding of bronze and the resonance of jade"; then additions and subtractions will attain what is appropriate. That the regions of the Jiang and Tuo rivers followed transformation, and the banks of the Ru River obeyed teaching, was the moral teaching and transformation of King Wen, yet in truth this was rooted …

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
於緝熈敬止華夏率俾丕單稱德武王之教化
也而實原於建用皇極曰敬止曰建極文武不
外乎此心也臣願
陛下以是心端教化之本表正萬邦建中于民參以
董子所謂正朝廷以正百官正百官以正萬民
則教化為益隆矣儆戒無虞者堯舜制治於未
亂也儆戒非出於是心乎臣願
陛下心堯舜儆戒之心事事務防微念念在杜漸則
致治方術之良在此矣兢業萬幾者堯舜保邦
於未危也兢業非出於此心乎臣願
===
陛下心堯舜兢業之心圖難於其易為大於其細則
保邦謨謀之遠在是矣詩曰不剛不柔敷政優
優古人為政之道未嘗偏於寬且猛也臣願
陛下精一執中寬不流於姑息猛不過於苛暴剛柔
相濟操縱相資則為政得其宜矣書曰二百里
奮武衞古人備邊之策未嘗有外於用武也臣
願
陛下選將以運謀練兵以奮武且耕且守来則拒之
往則勿追則備邊有其策矣人才國家之利器
也賢能固非爵祿可誘然足以為勸不肖固非

translation_en:
… in continuous bright reverence; that all within and beyond China followed and submitted, and the whole world praised his virtue—this was the moral transformation of King Wu, and in truth it originated in establishing and using the August Ultimate. Whether called "abiding in reverence" or "establishing the Ultimate," King Wen and King Wu did not go beyond this mind. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty take this mind to rectify the root of instruction and transformation, setting a standard to rectify the myriad states and establishing the mean among the people. If You consult what Master Dong [Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒] called "rectifying the court to rectify the hundred officials, and rectifying the hundred officials to rectify the myriad people," then instruction and transformation will become ever more flourishing.

Being vigilant when there is no cause for anxiety was how Yao and Shun established order before disorder arose. Does not vigilance issue from this mind? Your servant wishes that Your Majesty make the vigilant mind of Yao and Shun Your own mind, striving in every matter to guard against the subtle and keeping every thought on checking tendencies at their inception; then the excellence of the methods for achieving order will lie herein. Being cautious and reverent in the myriad affairs of state was how Yao and Shun preserved the state before peril arose. Does not caution and reverence issue from this mind? Your servant wishes that Your Majesty make the cautious and reverent mind of Yao and Shun Your own mind, tackling the difficult while it is easy and achieving the great through the minute; then the far-reaching counsels for preserving the state will lie herein.

The Book of Odes (Shi) says: "Neither harsh noryielding, he spreads his governance gently." The ancients' way of governing was never biased toward either leniency or severity. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty hold fast the mean with refined singleness of mind, so that leniency does not degenerate into lax indulgence and severity does not go to the excess of harsh cruelty; when firmness and gentleness complement one another and tightening and relaxing aid one another, governance will attain its proper measure.

The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Two hundred li are for exerting military might in defense." The ancients' strategy for frontier defense never lay outside the use of military strength. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty select generals to devise strategies and train soldiers to exert military might, combining farming with defense, repelling the enemy when they come and not pursuing them when they depart; then frontier defense will have its proper strategy.

Men of talent are the sharp instruments of the state. The worthy and able certainly cannot be enticed by noble ranks and emoluments, yet these suffice to serve as encouragement; the unworthy certainly cannot…

title: 景泰五年進士登科錄
text:
刑罰可威然足以示懲其要在乎君心之用舎
何如也臣願
陛下秉一心之公極用舎之當如書所謂任賢勿貳
去邪勿疑則賢者進不肖者退人才何有於不
賢乎刑賞人君之大柄也急於刑而緩於賞則
君子無所勸急於賞而緩於刑則小人無所懲
其要在乎君心之好尚何如也臣願
陛下執兩端之中酌可否之當如詩所謂不僭不濫
不敢怠遑則善者勸不肖者懲刑賞何有於不
可乎中庸曰致中和天地位焉萬物育焉是灾
===
祥感召之速不外乎此心也
陛下誠能戒懼謹獨以極中和之德則氣和形和而
天地之和應矣將見三光全而寒暑平五穀熟
而人民育至治之徵嘉祥之應不期而自至矣
書曰儆戒無虞無怠無荒四夷來王是夷狄向
背之故不出乎此心也
陛下誠能謹德賤貨以盡來遠之道則近說遠來而
威德之譽揚矣將見四夷咸賓八蠻通道自西
自東自南自北無思不服莫敢不來王莫敢不
來享矣夫事必貴於師古書所謂事不師古以

… [nor] are the unworthy truly overawed by punishments and penalties, yet these are sufficient to serve as a warning. The crux of the matter lies in how the ruler's mind decides whom to employ and whom to cast aside. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would uphold the impartiality of a single mind and achieve the utmost appropriateness in employment and dismissal—just as the Book of Documents (Shu) says, "Employ the worthy without duplicity; remove the wicked without hesitation." Then the worthy will advance and the unworthy will retreat; how could men of talent fail to be worthy?

Punishments and rewards are the great handles of authority of a ruler of men. If one is hasty in punishing and slow in rewarding, then noble men have nothing to encourage them; if one is hasty in rewarding and slow in punishing, then petty men have nothing to deter them. The crux of the matter lies in what the ruler's mind favors and esteems. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would hold fast to the mean between the two extremes and weigh the appropriateness of what is permissible and what is not—just as the Book of Odes (Shi) says, "Neither overstepping nor excessive, not daring to be indolent orremiss." Then the good will be encouraged and the unworthy deterred; how could punishments and rewards fail to be fitting?

The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) says, "When equilibrium and harmony are realized to the highest degree, Heaven and Earth will attain their proper order and all things will be nourished." Thus the swiftness with which disasters and auspicious omens are called forth goes no further than this mind. If Your Majesty can truly be cautious, apprehensive, and watchful over yourself when alone so as to reach the pinnacle of the virtue of equilibrium and harmony, then vital energy and physical form will be in harmony, and the harmony of Heaven and Earth will respond. We shall see the three luminaries intact and cold and heat balanced, the five grains ripening and the people nourished; the signs of supreme governance and the responses of auspicious omens will arrive of themselves without being sought.

The Book of Documents says, "Be cautious and vigilant when there is no cause for anxiety; do not be indolent, do not be dissolute, and the four surrounding tribes will come to acknowledge your kingship." Thus the reason the border tribes turn toward or away from us does not go beyond this mind. If Your Majesty can truly be careful of your virtue and disdain material goods so as to exhaust the way of attracting the distant, then those near at hand will rejoice and those far away will come, and the renown of your majesty and virtue will spread far and wide. We shall see the four tribes all coming as guests and the eight southern tribes opening up roads; from the west and from the east, from the south and from the north, none will think of not submitting, none will dare not to come to acknowledge your kingship, and none will dare not to come to present tribute.

陛下之策臣者，臣既畧陳之矣，然於終篇顓有獻焉。臣聞《易》曰：「聖人久於其道，而天下化成。」《書》曰：「常厥德，保厥位。」《中庸》曰：「至誠無息，不息則久，久則徵，徵則悠遠，悠遠則博厚，博厚則高明。」是知人主一心，貴於有常。天地常其覆載，故能生萬物而不息；日月常其照臨，故能運萬古而不已。陛下中天地而立，並日月而明，誠體其有常之德，純亦不已，至誠無息，則博厚配地，高明配天，悠久無疆，而雍煕泰和之治，將億萬斯年有隆而無替矣。臣干冒天威，不勝戰慄，臣謹對。

Yet in putting measures into practice, one must value suiting what is appropriate to the times; this is what the Book of Changes (Yi) calls "comprehending changes so that the people do not grow weary, and transforming things with spirit-like subtlety so that the people find them fitting." To examine antiquity yet recognize what certainly cannot serve as a model for the present, and to suit the present without merely clinging rigidly to antiquity—this lies solely in the application of Your Majesty's single mind.

As for the policy questions Your Majesty has posed to Your servant, Your servant has already briefly set forth his views on them; yet at the close of this essay, I venture a special offering. Your servant has heard that the Book of Changes says: "The sage perseveres long in his Way, and all under Heaven is transformed and brought to completion." The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Make constant your virtue to preserve your throne." The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) says: "Utmost sincerity is ceaseless. Being ceaseless, it is long-lasting; being long-lasting, it becomes manifest; being manifest, it reaches far and lasts long; reaching far and lasting long, it becomes broad and thick; being broad and thick, it becomes high and brilliant." From this we know that the single mind of the ruler values constancy. Because Heaven and Earth are constant in their overarching cover and sustaining support, they can generate the myriad things without cease; because the sun and moon are constant in their shining presence, they can revolve through ten thousand ages without end. Your Majesty stands centered between Heaven and Earth and matches the sun and moon in brilliance. If You truly embody their constant virtue, remaining pure and unending, with utmost sincerity that never ceases, then Your breadth and thickness will match Earth, Your height and brilliance will match Heaven, and Your endurance will be boundless; thus the governance of harmonious prosperity and supreme peace will flourish without decline for hundreds of millions of years! Your servant has offended Your Celestial Majesty and is overcome with trembling and awe. Your servant respectfully replies.
